idiom_name: owner object: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor or scope-exit hook (guard types for one-off actions)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: encapsulate the resource in one type whose constructor acquires it (failing without side effects if acquisition fails) and whose destructor or scope-exit hook releases it; expose only operations that are valid while the resource is held, never a public close(). Express the ownership policy where the language can (unique owner, refcounted owner, borrowed handle) so two objects cannot release the same resource. Where the language has no destructor, use the nearest lifetime-bound construct (with, using, use, defer, ensure) plus a callback helper that funnels the body through one release point, and keep explicit release for lifetimes that outlive a scope. Release actions must be idempotent and non-throwing; any operation whose failure must be observed (flush, commit, fsync) stays an explicit call before the owner dies.
code_sketch:
class Owner:                       # invariant: holds the resource or does not exist
    Owner(spec):
        self.handle = acquire(spec)    # failure => no owner object at all
    destroy(self):
        release(self.handle)           # non-throwing, exactly once

owner = Owner(spec)                # client
use(owner)                         # no release call on any path
pitfalls: Half-initialised owners (a public open()/close() pair, or a constructor that swallows acquisition failure) remove the invariant and bring the leaked handle back.
Copyable owners that share one handle cause double release; define copy/move semantics or make the owner non-copyable.
Destructors that perform failing or blocking work turn a leak class of bugs into a shutdown or deadlock class of bugs.

Wrong move: release a resource from a destructor while another thread still uses it -> the lifetime ends at the wrong owner and causes use-after-close or races -> instead transfer an explicit owner or lease to the thread that performs release.

Wrong move: rely on a GC finalizer or cleaner for a lock, lease or file descriptor -> collection timing is nondeterministic and can exhaust the resource pool -> instead use deterministic scope, with, or try-with-resources cleanup.

Wrong move: perform commit, fsync, or flush only in a destructor -> close-time errors cannot be reported safely during unwinding -> instead make the success operation explicit and reserve destruction for no-fail release or rollback.
